communityRules.auth1: Only signed-in people can post (Google or BAQUEANO account). There are no anonymous reviews.
communityRules.auth2: One active review per account. It can be edited, not multiplied.
communityRules.auth3: Creating fake reviews, using fictitious accounts, posting staff texts as if they were users’, altering ratings or averages, showing invented counts or using unauthorized testimonials is prohibited.
communityRules.auth4: The average, count and distribution are calculated automatically in the database using only approved reviews.
communityRules.dataPrivate: Never published: email, phone, password, address, internal identifiers, IP or tokens. The "What could we improve?" suggestion is read only by the team. Internally we keep your account identifier, sign-in method, date, moderation status, platform, edit history and the consent version, date and purpose.
communityRules.dataPublic: Shown publicly: your public name, your photo (only if you choose), your stars, your comment, the date and the authentication badge.
communityRules.honestText: BAQUEANO connects travelers directly with owners and service providers; it does not process bookings or payments yet. That is why reviews should not claim a booking was made through BAQUEANO, and the badge says "Signed-in BAQUEANO user", not "verified trip" or "verified purchase".
communityRules.legalNotice: This document describes how the platform works today. It is pending legal review to confirm compliance with Nicaragua’s Law 787 on Personal Data Protection and Law 842 on the Protection of Consumer and User Rights.
communityRules.metaDescription: How we publish, moderate and protect reviews of BAQUEANO: authenticity, respectful criticism, personal data and each user’s rights.
communityRules.metaTitle: Community Guidelines and Review Policy | BAQUEANO
communityRules.modList: Insults, threats or discriminatory language · spam, advertising or automated content · dangerous links · personal data of the author or others · impersonation · illegal content · repeated posts.
communityRules.modText: Every new or edited review stays "under review" until the team checks it. Respectful criticism is published even with a low rating. Only content that includes the following is rejected or hidden, with a recorded reason:
communityRules.modTrace: No review is deleted without a trace: every approval, rejection, hiding, reply or report is recorded with who did it, when and why.
communityRules.purposeText: Reviews of BAQUEANO describe what it was like to use the platform: finding places, planning or contacting a local business directly. They are different from Traveler experiences, which are about destinations. Each rating is kept separate and never mixed.
communityRules.replyText: The team can reply publicly. The reply appears separately and labeled "BAQUEANO’s reply" so it is never confused with the user’s comment.
communityRules.reportText: Any signed-in user can report a published review with a reason. Reporting does not hide the review automatically: the team reviews each report and records its decision.
communityRules.rightsText: From the reviews page you can see your review’s status, edit it (it goes back to review), withdraw it so it stops being shown, or delete it: we then erase the text, your name and your photo, keeping only the record that it existed and when it was deleted.

Linked to the mountainous north. Founder of the Praxis Group (1963); he introduced material informalism using soils, volcanic textures and scrap metal as a metaphor for Nicaragua’s landscape and socio-political reality.
pages.historia.artistas.items.bacon.mile: A pioneer of Afro-Caribbean contemporary dance and Caribbean ballroom dance; she connected Maypole (Palo de Mayo) folklore and Caribbean Coast rhythms with the stages of the Pacific.
pages.historia.artistas.items.beer.miles: The first Afro-descendant national painter from the Caribbean Coast. Her work is living testimony to Creole identity, Black Caribbean women and the community memory of Bluefields.
pages.historia.artistas.items.carrion.mi: A filmmaker who connects the collective historical memory of the 1980s with urban generational dilemmas through her documentary Heredera del viento.
pages.historia.artistas.items.deleon.mil: Creator of the scraped-wax and fresco-transparency technique. He founded the Museo-Galería 904 in the capital before the 1972 earthquake, capturing the lakeside light of Managua.
pages.historia.artistas.items.espinoza.m: Heir to León’s university intellectual tradition; her plays explore colonial memory, patriarchal oppression and the urban mythology of the country’s first capital.
pages.historia.artistas.items.gron.miles: She shaped the country’s civic monumental memory: the Andrés Castro monument at Hacienda San Jacinto (Tipitapa), the Rubén Darío relief and the statue of the chief Diriangén.
pages.historia.artistas.items.lopez.mile: A national reference in researching and documenting marimba sones, the danzas de negras, the bailes de húngaras and the choreographic mestizaje of Monimbó and Masaya.
pages.historia.artistas.items.marin.mile: Heir to the artistic tradition of the Meseta de los Pueblos; known for his visual architecture and dense palette-knife oil textures depicting Creole and urban Central American scenes.
pages.historia.artistas.items.montealegr: A witness through photojournalism to the insurrection, the National Literacy Crusade and post-war reconstruction; she captured everyday life in the capital’s working-class neighbourhoods.
pages.historia.artistas.items.morales.mi: Born in the “Great Sultana”. His imagery projects Lake Cocibolca, colonial still lifes and the lushness of the Nicaraguan Caribbean rainforest, carried onto the international circuit (Paris, New York).
pages.historia.artistas.items.penalba.lo: San Pedro de Lovago / San Juan de Oriente (ties to Masaya and León)
pages.historia.artistas.items.penalba.mi: Regarded as the father of modern painting in Nicaragua and director of the National School of Fine Arts; he steered the traditional and sacred iconography of the Pacific towards the expressionist avant-garde.
pages.historia.artistas.items.saenz.mile: The leading exponent of pictorial indigenism. He brought petroglyphs, pre-Columbian ceramics, northern legends and the line of the central highlands into contemporary murals and canvases.
pages.historia.artistas.items.saravia.mi: A founding figure of public art in the capital and Peñalba’s right hand at the Fine Arts school; he sculpted reliefs and figures that document mestizaje and the vernacular anatomy of the Pacific.

In 1987 Law No. 28, the Statute of Autonomy of the Regions of Nicaragua’s Caribbean Coast, was approved. The law symbolised the recognition of the ancestral rights of Indigenous and Afro-descendant peoples as the country’s multi-ethnic, multicultural and multilingual communities.
In 1502, on his fourth voyage, Christopher Columbus sailed along Nicaragua’s Caribbean coast and rounded a cape he named Gracias a Dios. In 1522, Gil González Dávila and Andrés Niño arrived overland from Panama and made contact with the chiefs Nicoya and Nicaragua. In 1524 the Spanish founded León and Granada, and in 1544 the territory became part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.costaCarib: The history of Nicaragua’s Caribbean followed its own path. In the 18th century the English allied with the Miskito people and consolidated their hold on the region; in 1748 they seized San Juan de Nicaragua. The Mosquitia, or Mosquito Coast, came to be regarded as an English colony until 1860, when the Treaty of Managua recognised Nicaragua’s sovereignty and created the Mosquitia Reserve.
The Caribbean Coast and the Mosquitia
pages.historia.audio.chapters.dario.text: Félix Rubén García Sarmiento was born in Metapa on 18 January 1867 and died in León on 6 February 1916. His father’s family was known as the Daríos, which is why he took the surname Darío. A poet, journalist and diplomat, he is regarded as the foremost representative of literary modernism in the Spanish language.
El Güegüense is a satirical drama, well known in Nicaragua, that brings together theatre, dance and music as a synthesis of Spanish and Indigenous cultures. It is performed every year at the feast of San Sebastián. UNESCO proclaimed it in 2005 and inscribed it in 2008 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.guerraNaci: Between 1855 and 1857, Nicaragua faced the filibuster incursion of William Walker. In the north, Generals Tomás Martínez and Fernando Chamorro organised the Army of the North (Ejército del Septentrión), whose officers declared in Matagalpa on 20 April 1856 that they would defend national independence to the last drop of blood. Six months of that resistance led to the Battle of San Jacinto.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.independen: The first independence uprisings broke out in 1811 in León, Granada and Rivas, with strong popular support. The Captaincy General of Guatemala, which included Nicaragua, declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821. A year later it was annexed to Agustín de Iturbide’s short-lived Mexican Empire, and in 1823 Nicaragua joined the Federation of the United Provinces of Central America.
León, one of the cities founded by the Spanish in 1524, was moved to its current site in 1610 after an earthquake. The ruins of the original city, known as León Viejo, were added to UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2000.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.patrimonio: Nicaragua has two properties on UNESCO’s World Heritage List: the Ruins of León Viejo, inscribed in 2000, and León Cathedral, inscribed in 2011.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.pueblosOri: When the Spanish arrived, Nicaragua’s Pacific region was already home to several peoples: the Maribios or Sutiavas, the Mangues or Chorotegas, and the Nahuas or Nicaraguas. They lived in farming villages on plains near the lakes and volcanoes, were governed by councils of elders or by chiefs, and traded by barter with neighbouring peoples. Their roots are linked to migrations from the north, from lands in present-day Mexico.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.sanJacinto: On Sunday, 14 September 1856, at the San Jacinto hacienda, Colonel José Dolores Estrada and his troops held off the filibusters’ attack. The fighting was hand to hand, and Andrés Castro, with no time to load his rifle, brought down a filibuster with a stone. A flanking sortie surprised the attackers, who fled. That same day, Estrada reported the victory in his official dispatch.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.sandino.te: Augusto Nicolás Calderón Sandino was born in Niquinohomo, Masaya, on 18 May 1895. In 1927 he began the armed struggle against the United States intervention at the head of the Army in Defence of National Sovereignty. He was assassinated on 21 February 1934 by National Guard officers acting on the orders of Anastasio Somoza García.
pages.historia.audio.chapters.treintaAno: After William Walker’s filibuster incursion, the Nicaraguan State slowly took shape. This period is known as the Thirty Years: it runs from the administrations of General Tomás Martínez, between 1858 and 1867, to 1893, the year of the liberal revolution.

pages.miNegocio.faqList.div1: Does Baqueano charge any commission on my sales?
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div10: Payment is 100% direct: the explorer coordinates with you by WhatsApp, email or phone, and pays however you both prefer (cash, transfer, bank deposit). Baqueano shows your direct contact on your profile. There is no intermediary payment gateway. Integration with Tilopay/BAC will soon be available for those who want it, but always optional and without Baqueano commissions.
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div11: Can I update my business information later?
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div12: Yes. Once your registration is approved, you'll get access to a management portal where you can update prices, schedules, photos and availability. Changes go through a quick review by the Administrator (usually less than 24 hours) before appearing in the app and on the website.
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div2: No. The Baqueano model is designed to eliminate financial intermediation. The explorer pays your cooperative or business directly. Baqueano facilitates the connection but does not touch or retain any percentage of your income. This is what we call "tourism with rural sovereignty".
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div3: Do I need INTUR registration to join?
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div4: It is not a strict requirement to sign up, but it is highly recommended. INTUR registration gives you access to the incentive regime of Laws No. 1210 and 1211, which promote community tourism development. The Baqueano team can guide you through INTUR registration if you need it.
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div5: How long until my business appears in the app?
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div6: Once your request is sent, the General Administrator reviews it in the Ops Center within 48-72 business hours. If the information is correct and verifiable, your business is published on the web map and in the Android app. You'll receive a confirmation email with your official host badge.
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div7: What is the trail GPS beacon system?
pages.miNegocio.faqList.div8: GPS beacons are satellite safety points that baqueano guides activate in the Android app when starting a tour. Explorers and their emergency contacts can see the location in real time. If an incident occurs, the SOS feature sends exact coordinates to emergency numbers and to the Baqueano Desk's WhatsApp.

pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p1: A summary of the most important things you should know about using BAQUEANO.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p2: It connects travelers with destinations, experiences and local providers in Nicaragua.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p3: Services are offered by local entrepreneurs, guides, cooperatives and businesses.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p4: Availability, prices and conditions are managed by each provider or through partners.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p5: The verified seal means the business has gone through our internal validation process; it is not a state certification.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p6: It gives recommendations and creates personalized routes. It may contain errors and does not replace official sources.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p7: It is a complementary tool for guidance and contact with local emergency services.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p8: We care for your personal information under our strict Privacy Policy, with no selling to third parties.
pages.terminos.termSummarySection.p9: We promote sustainable tourism that respects communities, culture and the environment.
